children.text: Windows 11 Pro vs Home is one of the most common licensing questions we get. Both editions share the same core experience, but Pro unlocks a set of business and security features that Home cannot run. Here's what actually differs, what it costs, and how to pick the right license for your PC.

Quick answer: buy Windows 11 Home if you mostly browse, stream, and game. Choose Windows 11 Pro if you need full BitLocker encryption, Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V or Windows Sandbox, or a work domain — or if you're building a workstation that exceeds 128 GB of RAM.
Windows 11 Pro vs Home: Key Differences

The short version: Windows 11 Home is built for everyday personal use. Windows 11 Pro adds features aimed at professionals, small businesses, and power users — full BitLocker encryption, Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V virtualization, Windows Sandbox, and the ability to join a domain or Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD). Microsoft's own
edition comparison
lists the differences side by side.
BitLocker drive encryption (full control, plus BitLocker To Go for external drives)
Remote Desktop: host incoming connections to your PC
Hyper-V: run virtual machines natively
Windows Sandbox: test untrusted software in an isolated environment
Domain join and Microsoft Entra ID join for business networks
Group Policy Editor and mobile device management (MDM) enrollment

At a glance: both editions include the same core apps, the same interface, and the same security baseline. Home is the edition that ships on most consumer laptops and desktops. Pro is the edition businesses buy, and it is also the edition most power users choose when they build their own machine, because it removes the artificial limits Home places on encryption, remote access, virtualization, and hardware.
What Both Editions Share

Don't assume Home is stripped down. Both Windows 11 Home and Pro include the full modern Windows 11 experience: the redesigned Start menu, Snap Layouts, Copilot, Auto HDR and DirectStorage for gaming, Windows Hello biometric sign-in, Secure Boot, device encryption, parental controls, Windows Security, and passkey support.

The security baseline is also the same. Both editions require TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot, and both include Microsoft Defender antivirus, firewall and network protection, and core isolation. The difference is depth: Home gives you automatic device encryption when you sign in with a Microsoft account, while Pro gives you full BitLocker management.
Features Only in Windows 11 Pro
BitLocker and device encryption

Windows 11 Home includes basic device encryption, but it's automatic and tied to a Microsoft account. Windows 11 Pro includes BitLocker Drive Encryption, which lets you manage encryption manually, protect external drives with BitLocker To Go, and set your own recovery options. If you carry sensitive files on a laptop, this is the single most compelling reason to choose Pro.
Remote Desktop

With Windows 11 Home, you can use the Remote Desktop app to connect out to other PCs, but you cannot host incoming connections. Windows 11 Pro turns your PC into a Remote Desktop host, so you can access your machine from another computer, phone, or tablet. If you regularly work from home or travel, that's a real productivity win.
Hyper-V and Windows Sandbox

Hyper-V is Microsoft's built-in virtualization platform, included in Windows 11 Pro, Enterprise, and Education. It lets you run Linux, older Windows versions, or test environments in virtual machines. Windows Sandbox gives you a disposable, isolated Windows session for opening files or software you don't fully trust. Both are Pro-only.
Domain join, Group Policy, and management

Windows 11 Pro can join an Active Directory domain or Microsoft Entra ID, which is how most businesses manage fleets of PCs. It also includes the Local Group Policy Editor and supports mobile device management enrollment. Home has none of these — which is fine for a personal machine, but a blocker for work devices.
Price: How Much Does Each Edition Cost?

Microsoft's list prices are $139.99 for Windows 11 Home and $199.99 for Windows 11 Pro. Upgrading from Home to Pro through the Microsoft Store costs about $99. If you're building a PC or buying a standalone license, the retail price gap is roughly $60 — and many authorized resellers sell genuine Windows 11 Pro keys for less than Microsoft's list price. If you're coming from Windows 10, the upgrade to Windows 11 is free for the equivalent edition — Windows 10 Pro upgrades to Windows 11 Pro, and Windows 10 Home to Windows 11 Home. Windows 10 reached
end of support on October 14, 2025
, so moving to Windows 11 is the recommended path for continued security updates.
Hardware Limits: RAM and CPU

Both editions run on the same minimum hardware: a 1 GHz dual-core 64-bit processor, 4 GB of RAM, 64 GB of storage, UEFI with Secure Boot, and TPM 2.0. But Pro supports more powerful hardware. Windows 11 Home tops out at 128 GB of RAM and 64 CPU cores, while Pro supports up to 2 TB of RAM, 128 cores, and dual CPUs. For almost everyone this doesn't matter — but for workstation builds it does. Microsoft publishes the full
system requirements
for both editions.
Should You Upgrade from Home to Pro?
Choose Windows 11 Pro if you:
Encrypt drives with BitLocker or manage encryption centrally
Need to remote into your own PC from elsewhere
Run virtual machines with Hyper-V or want Windows Sandbox
Join a company domain or Microsoft Entra ID
Manage devices with Group Policy or MDM
Build a workstation with more than 128 GB of RAM

Choose Windows 11 Home if you mostly browse, stream, game, and do everyday tasks on a single personal PC. Home covers those scenarios well, and you can always upgrade to Pro later without reinstalling Windows.
How to Upgrade from Windows 11 Home to Pro
There are two ways to upgrade Windows 11 Home to Pro, and neither requires reinstalling Windows. Microsoft's
official upgrade guide
walks through both options.
Upgrade through the Microsoft Store: open Settings > System > Activation, select Upgrade your edition of Windows, and follow the Store flow to purchase and apply the upgrade.
Enter a Windows 11 Pro product key: go to Settings > System > Activation > Change product key, enter a valid key, and Windows upgrades the edition in place — your files, apps, and settings are kept.

If you buy a Pro key from a reseller, make sure it's a genuine license. After you enter a valid Windows 11 Pro key, Windows activates online automatically. If activation fails, the built-in Windows Activation troubleshooter can help you resolve it.
OEM vs Retail: Which Windows 11 Pro License Should You Buy?

When you buy Windows 11 Pro, you'll see two main license types. An OEM (original equipment manufacturer) license is tied to the first motherboard it's activated on — it's the cheapest way to license a PC you build yourself, but you can't transfer it to a new machine later. A retail license can be moved to a new PC when you upgrade hardware, which is why it costs more.
Both types activate the same Windows 11 Pro edition with the same features. Choose an
OEM key
for a self-built PC you plan to keep, and a
retail license
if you expect to transfer the license to future hardware.
Windows 11 Pro vs Home: FAQ
Is Windows 11 Pro worth it for home users?

For most home users, no. Windows 11 Home covers browsing, streaming, gaming, and everyday productivity. Pro becomes worth the extra cost when you want full BitLocker encryption, Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V, or Windows Sandbox — or when you simply want the edition with no hardware limits.
Can I upgrade from Windows 11 Home to Pro without reinstalling?

Yes. Enter a Windows 11 Pro product key under Settings > System > Activation > Change product key, or buy the upgrade through the Microsoft Store. Windows upgrades the edition in place and keeps your files, apps, and settings.
Is Windows 11 Pro faster than Home?
No. On the same hardware, Windows 11 Home and Pro perform identically for everyday tasks and gaming. The differences are features and limits, not speed.
Does Windows 11 Home include BitLocker?

Not the full version. Windows 11 Home includes automatic device encryption when you sign in with a Microsoft account, but you can't manage encryption manually, use BitLocker To Go on external drives, or control recovery options. Those capabilities are part of Windows 11 Pro.
Can I use one Windows 11 Pro license on more than one PC?
No — one license covers one PC. A
retail license
can be transferred to a new PC when you upgrade hardware, while an OEM license is tied to the first motherboard. If you need Pro on two machines, you need two keys.
Is Windows 11 Pro a subscription?

No. Windows 11 Pro is a one-time purchase, not a subscription. A retail or OEM license includes feature and security updates for as long as your PC is supported, with no recurring fee. A Microsoft 365 subscription is a separate, optional purchase for Office apps and cloud features.
The Bottom Line

For most home users, Windows 11 Home is enough. Choose Windows 11 Pro if you need BitLocker, Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V, or business management features — or if you simply want the most capable edition and don't want to think about limits later. The extra cost is modest, and a
genuine Windows 11 Pro key
is a one-time purchase that lasts for the life of your PC.
